modules.title: Introduction to Java and OOPs
modules.description: Introduction to Java and OOPs covers the foundational concepts of object-oriented programming in Java. This module helps beginners understand the basics of classes, objects, and other fundamental OOP principles in the Java context.

topics.title: What is OOPs / Features of OOPs
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

pages.title: Introduction to Object Oriented Programming
pages.content:
Object-oriented programming (OOP) organizes a program around objects that combine state and behavior. In Java, a class defines the structure and behavior, while an object is a runtime instance of that class.

The main OOP ideas used throughout this course are encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and abstraction. These ideas help separate responsibilities, protect internal state, and make related behavior easier to extend.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Introduction to Object Oriented Programming explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Student { String name; Student(String n){name=n;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){ Student s=new Student("Asha"); System.out.println(s.name); } }

checkpoint.question: In What is OOPs / Features of OOPs, which statement best describes Introduction to Object Oriented Programming?
options: It applies the Java mechanism needed for Introduction to Object Oriented Programming while keeping the class design and runtime behavior explicit.
It requires global mutable state shared by unrelated classes.
It disables compile-time type checking to simplify execution.
It depends on unbounded recursion for every object operation.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Introduction to Object Oriented Programming without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: Access Modifiers in Java
pages.content:
Java controls member visibility with access modifiers. `public` allows access from anywhere, `private` restricts access to the declaring class, `protected` allows package access plus access from subclasses, and no modifier gives package-private access.

Choosing the narrowest visibility that satisfies the design is an important encapsulation practice. Private state is commonly exposed through methods such as getters and validated setters.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Access Modifiers in Java explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Student { private int age; void setAge(int a){age=a;} int getAge(){return age;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Student s=new Student();s.setAge(20);System.out.println(s.getAge());}}

pages.title: How to deal with Private Data Member
pages.content:
A private field cannot be accessed directly from unrelated classes. A getter provides read access and a setter can provide controlled write access.

A setter can also enforce an invariant before changing the field. This keeps validation close to the data it protects instead of spreading validation across callers.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to deal with Private Data Member explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Account { private int balance; void deposit(int x){balance+=x;} int getBalance(){return balance;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Account x=new Account();x.deposit(100);System.out.println(x.getBalance());}}

pages.title: Instance Variable
pages.content:
An instance variable belongs to an object rather than to the class as a whole. Every object gets its own copy of each instance field.

Instance variables are typically declared without `static` and are accessed through an object reference. Two objects of the same class can therefore hold different values for the same field.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Instance Variable explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Counter { int value; Counter(int v){value=v;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Counter c=new Counter(5);System.out.println(c.value);}}

pages.title: Syntax to declare a class
pages.content:
A Java class is declared with the `class` keyword, followed by the class name and a body enclosed in braces. The body can contain fields, constructors, methods, and nested types.

For a public top-level class, the source file name must match the public class name. Inside the class body, members can be given appropriate access modifiers.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Syntax to declare a class explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Car { String model; Car(String m){model=m;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Car("Sedan").model);}}

pages.title: Object Reference Sharing
pages.content:
A Java variable holding an object stores a reference to that object. Assigning one object reference to another does not copy the object; both references point to the same instance.

Consequently, a mutation performed through one reference is visible through the other reference. Creating an independent object requires a separate construction or explicit copying strategy.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Object Reference Sharing explains a Java design rule used in What is OOPs / Features of OOPs.

codeCard.code: class Counter { int value; Counter(int v){value=v;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Counter c1=new Counter(5);Counter c2=c1;c1.value++;System.out.println(c2.value);}}

pages.title: Static in Java
pages.content:
A `static` member belongs to the class rather than to one particular object. A static field has one shared value for the class, and a static method can be called without creating an instance.

Static initialization blocks run when the class is initialized. Static nested classes are also associated with the outer class rather than with an outer instance.

callout.text: Static in Java explains a Java design rule used in Constructors, static members.

codeCard.code: class Counter { static int count; Counter(){count++;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Counter();new Counter();System.out.println(Counter.count);}}

pages.title: Multiple Choice Question
pages.content:
This page reinforces the surrounding topic with a focused concept check. Pay attention to what belongs to the class, what belongs to an object, and what the Java compiler requires.

Read the example carefully before answering: the goal is to connect the syntax to the runtime behavior it produces.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Multiple Choice Question explains a Java design rule used in Constructors, static members.

codeCard.code: class MathBox { static int square(int x){return x*x;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(MathBox.square(6));}}

pages.title: Constructor vs Methods
pages.content:
A constructor initializes a newly created object and has the same name as its class with no return type. It is invoked as part of object creation.

A regular method represents behavior that can be invoked after an object exists. Methods have a return type (or `void`), can have arbitrary names, and are not limited to object initialization.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Constructor vs Methods explains a Java design rule used in Constructors, static members.

codeCard.code: class Person { String name; Person(String n){name=n;} void greet(){System.out.println("Hello "+name);} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Person p=new Person("Ravi");p.greet();}}

pages.title: User Defined vs Default Constructor
pages.content:
If a class declares no constructor, Java supplies a no-argument default constructor. Once a class declares its own constructor, that automatic default constructor is no longer supplied.

When both no-argument and parameterized construction are required, declare both constructors explicitly.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: User Defined vs Default Constructor explains a Java design rule used in Constructors, static members.

codeCard.code: class Box { int x; Box(int x){this.x=x;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Box b=new Box(7);System.out.println(b.x);}}

pages.title: Inheritance in Java
pages.content:
Inheritance lets a subclass reuse accessible members of a superclass. Java class inheritance uses `extends`, and each class has one direct superclass.

Inheritance is most useful when the child truly represents a specialized form of the parent. Reused state or behavior should still remain appropriately encapsulated.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Inheritance in Java explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class Person { String name="Asha"; } class Student extends Person {} public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Student().name);}}

checkpoint.question: In Inheritance in Java, which statement best describes Inheritance in Java?
options: It applies the Java mechanism needed for Inheritance in Java while keeping the class design and runtime behavior explicit.
It requires global mutable state shared by unrelated classes.
It disables compile-time type checking to simplify execution.
It depends on unbounded recursion for every object operation.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Inheritance in Java without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: Constructor Call Order
pages.content:
When an object of a subclass is created, the superclass constructor runs before the subclass constructor. A no-argument `super()` call is inserted when appropriate.

This ordering ensures that inherited state is initialized before subclass-specific initialization begins.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Constructor Call Order explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class A { A(){System.out.println("A");} } class B extends A { B(){System.out.println("B");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new B();}}

pages.title: Calling Superclass Constructor
pages.content:
A subclass constructor can explicitly call a superclass constructor with `super(...)`. The `super(...)` call must be the first statement in the constructor.

This is useful when the parent class requires parameters to initialize its own state.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Calling Superclass Constructor explains a Java design rule used in Inheritance in Java.

codeCard.code: class Person { String name; Person(String n){name=n;} } class Student extends Person { Student(String n){super(n);} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Student("Anu").name);}}

pages.title: Example of Aggregation
pages.content:
Aggregation represents a “has-a” relationship in which one object refers to another object that can exist independently.

For example, a Department can hold a reference to a Teacher without owning the Teacher's lifetime. The two classes therefore have separate responsibilities and can be reused independently.

Aggregation keeps related objects loosely connected. It supports reuse because the aggregated object can be created separately and supplied to multiple consumers.

This relationship is often preferable to inheritance when the relationship is about collaboration rather than specialization.

pages.title: Polymorphism in Java
pages.content:
Polymorphism lets one interface or parent type represent objects of different concrete classes. Java supports compile-time polymorphism through method overloading and runtime polymorphism through method overriding.

The declared type controls which members are visible, while runtime dispatch selects an overridden instance method implementation.

pages.title: Function Overloading
pages.content:
Method overloading defines multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists. The compiler chooses the matching overload from the argument types and count.

Changing only the return type is not enough to overload a method.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Function Overloading explains a Java design rule used in Polymorphism in Java.

pages.content:
Constructors can also be overloaded. A class may provide several constructors with different parameter lists so callers can create objects with different initialization options.

Each constructor should establish a valid object state and avoid unnecessary duplicated initialization logic.

pages.content:
Overloading provides a consistent operation name for related inputs. Callers can use the same method name while the compiler selects the appropriate parameter signature.

This can improve readability when the overloaded operations represent the same conceptual behavior.

topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Method overriding in Java.

pages.title: Method Overriding
pages.content:
Overriding occurs when a subclass provides a new implementation of an inherited instance method with a compatible signature.

Using `@Override` lets the compiler verify that the method actually overrides a superclass method.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Method Overriding explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class A { String get(){return "A";} } class B extends A { String get(){return "B";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new B().get());}}

checkpoint.question: In Method overriding in Java, which statement best describes Method Overriding?
options: It applies the Java mechanism needed for Method Overriding while keeping the class design and runtime behavior explicit.
It requires global mutable state shared by unrelated classes.
It disables compile-time type checking to simplify execution.
It depends on unbounded recursion for every object operation.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Method Overriding without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: How to override methods in Java
pages.content:
To override a method, keep the same method name and compatible parameter list in the subclass. The return type must be compatible, and visibility cannot be reduced.

The `@Override` annotation is recommended because it catches common signature mistakes during compilation.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to override methods in Java explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Animal { void sound(){System.out.println("sound");} } class Dog extends Animal { @Override void sound(){System.out.println("bark");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Dog().sound();}}

pages.title: Overriding Final Method
pages.content:
A method declared `final` cannot be overridden by a subclass. This is useful when a class must guarantee one implementation for a particular operation.

A subclass can still define a different method with a different signature, but that is overloading or a separate method, not overriding.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Overriding Final Method explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Base { final void show(){System.out.println("base");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Base().show();}}

pages.title: Method Overriding Access Modifiers
pages.content:
An overriding method may keep or widen visibility, but it cannot reduce the superclass method's accessibility.

For example, a `protected` method can be overridden as `protected` or `public`, but not as `private`.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Method Overriding Access Modifiers explains a Java design rule used in Method overriding in Java.

codeCard.code: class Base { protected void show(){System.out.println("base");} } class Child extends Base { @Override public void show(){System.out.println("child");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Child().show();}}

pages.title: Method Overriding Requirements in Java
pages.content:
For true overriding, the subclass method must match the inherited instance method's signature and obey Java's access and exception rules.

Static methods are hidden rather than overridden, and constructors are never overridden.

topics.title: Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

pages.title: Interfaces in Java
pages.content:
An interface defines a contract that implementing classes must satisfy. A class uses `implements` and provides implementations for the interface's abstract methods unless the class itself is abstract.

A class can implement multiple interfaces, which is Java's standard mechanism for combining multiple contracts.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Interfaces in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: interface Printable { void print(); } class Report implements Printable { public void print(){System.out.println("report");} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Report().print();}}

checkpoint.question: Which design choice is consistent with Interfaces in Java?
options: Use the feature for the responsibility it is intended to model, and preserve valid object invariants.
Expose every field as a public global variable.
Replace every method with static state.
Avoid all compiler diagnostics.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Interfaces in Java without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: How to use Interfaces in Java
pages.content:
Program to the interface type when possible. Store an implementation object in an interface reference so the caller depends on the contract rather than a concrete class.

This makes implementations replaceable and supports runtime polymorphism.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to use Interfaces in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: interface Pay { int amount(); } class Cash implements Pay { public int amount(){return 100;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Pay p=new Cash();System.out.println(p.amount());}}

pages.title: Abstract Class
pages.content:
An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly. It can contain fields, constructors, concrete methods, and abstract methods.

A concrete subclass must implement the inherited abstract methods unless the subclass is also abstract.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Shape { abstract int area(); } class Square extends Shape { int x; Square(int x){this.x=x;} int area(){return x*x;} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Square(5).area());}}

pages.title: Purpose of Abstract Methods
pages.content:
An abstract method specifies behavior that subclasses must provide without supplying the implementation itself.

This allows the base class to define a common API while leaving subclass-specific behavior to concrete types.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Purpose of Abstract Methods explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Animal { abstract String sound(); } class Dog extends Animal { String sound(){return "bark";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){System.out.println(new Dog().sound());}}

pages.title: Abstract Class Constructors in Java
pages.content:
An abstract class can have constructors even though the class itself cannot be instantiated. The constructor runs as part of constructing a concrete subclass.

This is useful for initializing state shared by all subclasses.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class Constructors in Java explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Base { Base(){System.out.println("base");} } class Child extends Base { } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){new Child();}}

pages.title: Abstract Class Characteristics
pages.content:
Abstract classes support partial implementation and shared state. They are useful when related classes need common behavior as well as one or more required operations.

Use an abstract class when there is a meaningful common base implementation; use interfaces for contracts that may cut across unrelated class hierarchies.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Abstract Class Characteristics explains a Java design rule used in Interfaces & Abstract classes in Java.

codeCard.code: abstract class Vehicle { abstract String type(); } class Car extends Vehicle { String type(){return "car";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Vehicle v=new Car();System.out.println(v.type());}}

pages.title: Dot Operator in Nested Classes
pages.content:
The dot operator is used to access static nested types from the outer class, for example `Outer.Inner`.

For a non-static inner class, an outer instance is required before the inner object can be created.

pages.title: Object Creation and Output
pages.content:
Objects are created with `new`, which allocates and initializes an instance. The resulting reference can be used to invoke methods or access accessible fields.

Constructors run during object creation before control returns to the caller.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Object Creation and Output explains a Java design rule used in Returning objects - Static, nested and inner classes.

pages.title: Nested Class Keyword in Java
pages.content:
A nested class is declared inside another class. A static nested class does not need an outer instance, while a non-static inner class is associated with one.

Nested types are useful for grouping implementation details that belong closely to an enclosing class.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Nested Class Keyword in Java explains a Java design rule used in Returning objects - Static, nested and inner classes.

codeCard.code: class Outer { class Inner { int value(){return 9;} } } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Outer o=new Outer();System.out.println(o.new Inner().value());}}

pages.title: Static methods in Java
pages.content:
Static methods belong to the class and do not have an implicit `this` reference. They can directly access static members but need an object reference to access instance state.

Static methods are suitable for operations that do not depend on a particular object's fields.

pages.title: Advantage of Upcasting
pages.content:
Upcasting stores a subclass object in a superclass reference. The code can then work with a general API while the concrete object remains specialized.

This supports flexible method calls and is a common foundation for runtime polymorphism.

pages.title: Upcasting Usage
pages.content:
Upcasting is implicit when a subclass object is assigned to a superclass reference. Only members visible through the superclass type can be accessed directly.

Overridden instance methods still dispatch to the subclass implementation at runtime.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Upcasting Usage explains a Java design rule used in Upcasting & Dynamic method dispatch.

codeCard.code: class Animal { String sound(){return "sound";} } class Dog extends Animal { String sound(){return "bark";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Animal a1=new Dog();System.out.println(a1.sound());}}

pages.title: Benefit of dynamic method dispatch
pages.content:
Dynamic method dispatch allows Java to choose an overridden instance method at runtime according to the actual object.

This makes code that depends on a parent type extensible: new subclasses can provide behavior without changing the caller.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Benefit of dynamic method dispatch explains a Java design rule used in Upcasting & Dynamic method dispatch.

codeCard.code: class A { String show(){return "A";} } class B extends A { String show(){return "B";} } public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){A x=new B();System.out.println(x.show());}}

pages.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch Behavior
pages.content:
When a parent reference points to a child object, an overridden instance method call uses the child implementation. This is runtime polymorphism.

The declared reference type still determines which methods the compiler allows the call site to access.

pages.title: Exception handling in Java
pages.content:
Exceptions represent abnormal conditions that a program may recover from or report. Java uses `try`, `catch`, `throw`, and `finally` to structure exception handling.

Good exception handling keeps recovery logic close to the operation that can fail and avoids silently hiding unexpected errors.

codeCard.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){try{throw new Exception("x");}catch(Exception e){System.out.println("handled");}}}

Replace every method with static state.
Avoid all compiler diagnostics.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Exception handling in Java without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: How to use Try, Catch and Throw
pages.content:
A `try` block contains code that may fail, a `catch` block handles a matching exception, and `throw` explicitly raises an exception.

Use exceptions for exceptional conditions rather than ordinary control flow.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to use Try, Catch and Throw explains a Java design rule used in Exception handling basics.

codeCard.code: public class Main { static void check(int x)throws Exception{if(x<0)throw new Exception();} public static void main(String[] a){try{check(1);System.out.println("ok");}catch(Exception e){System.out.println("bad");}}}

pages.title: Difference between Exception and Errors
pages.content:
Both `Exception` and `Error` inherit from `Throwable`, but they represent different categories. Exceptions generally describe conditions application code may handle, while errors usually indicate serious JVM or environment problems.

Not every throwable should be caught and ignored.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Difference between Exception and Errors explains a Java design rule used in Exception handling basics.

codeCard.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){try{int x=1/0;System.out.println(x);}catch(ArithmeticException e){System.out.println("exception");}}}

pages.title: Checked and Unchecked Exceptions
pages.content:
Checked exceptions must be handled or declared by the compiler. Unchecked exceptions are subclasses of `RuntimeException` and do not require that declaration.

Choose exception types that accurately describe whether the caller can reasonably recover from the condition.

pages.title: Processes and Threads
pages.content:
A process is an independent running program with its own memory space. Threads are execution paths within a process and share the process's memory.

Threads are lighter than processes but introduce synchronization concerns when shared state is accessed concurrently.

pages.content:
Java supports concurrent execution through `Thread`, `Runnable`, executors, and related APIs. A thread should have a clear unit of work and a well-defined lifecycle.

Concurrency improves responsiveness or throughput for suitable workloads, but shared mutable state must be coordinated carefully.

Sleeping does not release intrinsic locks held by the thread. Use it for timing or demonstration, not as a synchronization mechanism.

pages.title: How to interrupt threads in Java
pages.content:
Thread interruption is cooperative. Calling `interrupt()` sets the interrupted status, and blocking operations may respond by throwing `InterruptedException`.

Worker code should check interruption and exit promptly instead of relying on forced thread termination.

callout.text: How to interrupt threads in Java explains a Java design rule used in Yield method and Interupting a thread.

codeCard.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] a)throws Exception{Thread t=new Thread(()->{while(!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()){};});t.start();t.interrupt();t.join();System.out.println("interrupted");}}

pages.title: How to interrupt and stop a thread
pages.content:
A long-running worker should periodically check its interrupted status and use that signal to leave its loop.

The safe pattern is cooperative cancellation: request interruption, let the worker finish or clean up, and then join it when the caller needs completion.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: How to interrupt and stop a thread explains a Java design rule used in Yield method and Interupting a thread.

codeCard.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] a)throws Exception{Thread t=new Thread(()->{while(!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted())Thread.yield();});t.start();t.interrupt();t.join();System.out.println("stopped");}}

pages.title: How to interrupt thread that doesnot stop working
pages.content:
A thread that ignores interruption can continue running indefinitely. Responsive workers must make sure their loops, waits, and blocking operations cooperate with interruption.

For CPU-bound loops, checking `isInterrupted()` regularly is essential.

callout.text: How to interrupt thread that doesnot stop working explains a Java design rule used in Yield method and Interupting a thread.

The synchronization policy should protect the invariant rather than merely surround arbitrary code.

pages.title: Generic Programming
pages.content:
Generics let a class or method work with a family of reference types while preserving compile-time type safety.

For example, `Box<String>` stores strings, while `Box<Integer>` stores integers. The compiler checks that the declared type is used consistently.

codeCard.code: class Box<T>{T value;Box(T v){value=v;}T get(){return value;}} public class Main { public static void main(String[] a){Box<String> b=new Box<>("Java");System.out.println(b.get());}}

checkpoint.question: What should you verify when applying Generic Programming in Java?
options: The declaration, visibility, and runtime behavior must match the rules of Generic Programming.
All members must be public.
Every class must inherit from two concrete classes.
Exceptions should always be ignored.
checkpoint.explanation: The correct choice applies the Java/OOP rule associated with Generic Programming without introducing unrelated state or unsafe behavior.

pages.title: Generic Methods
pages.content:
A generic method declares its type parameter before the return type, such as `<T> T first(T a, T b)`.

Type inference often lets the caller omit the type argument, while the compiler still checks the operations permitted for the type parameter.

callout.title: Key Concept
callout.text: Generic Methods explains a Java design rule used in Generic programming: classes, methods.

codeCard.code: public class Main { static <T> void show(T x){System.out.println(x);} public static void main(String[] a){show("Java");}}

pages.title: How to use Generic Methods
pages.content:
Generic methods are useful when the same operation should work for many types without duplicated implementations.

When the method needs specific capabilities, a bounded type parameter such as `<T extends Number>` can constrain the accepted types while retaining genericity.

Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.

questions.question: Question 2: What is the correct Java principle for readers and writers?
options: Character streams such as Reader and Writer are suited to text.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: Character streams such as Reader and Writer are suited to text.

Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: Resources that implement AutoCloseable can be closed automatically.

questions.question: Question 5: Which statement best describes read and write modes in Generics and File handling?

Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: Opening an output stream for append preserves existing content and adds new data.

questions.question: Question 6: What is the correct Java principle for text processing?
options: File content can be read, transformed, and written to another destination.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: File content can be read, transformed, and written to another destination.

questions.question: Question 7: Which option demonstrates correct understanding of generic types?
options: A parameterized type such as `Box<String>` preserves the element type.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: A parameterized type such as `Box<String>` preserves the element type.

questions.question: Question 8: Why is generic methods used in Java?
options: A method can declare its own type parameter and infer it from arguments.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: A method can declare its own type parameter and infer it from arguments.

questions.question: Question 9: Which statement best describes upper bounds in Generics and File handling?
options: A bound such as `<T extends Number>` restricts the type while retaining genericity.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: A bound such as `<T extends Number>` restricts the type while retaining genericity.

questions.question: Question 10: What is the correct Java principle for type safety?
options: Generics move many type errors from runtime to compile time.
Make every member public so any class can change it.
Disable compiler checks and rely on runtime guesses.
Use unrelated global state for every object.
questions.explanation: Generics move many type errors from runtime to compile time.
